program_overview.title: A Level Computer Science for AQA 7517 and OCR H446
program_overview.tagline: Two boards, one discipline: write real Python, explain the theory in the words examiners mark, and run your own project with a method you understand.
program_overview.description:
Two English exam boards set most A Level Computer Science entries, and they examine the same subject in different shapes. AQA's A Level 7517 has two exams worth 40% each and a project worth 20%. AQA's Paper 1 is an "On-screen exam: 2 hours 30 minutes" in which "Students answer a series of short questions and write/adapt/extend programs in an Electronic Answer Document", and AQA says it will "issue Preliminary Material, a Skeleton Program (available in each of the Programming Languages) and, where appropriate, test data, for use in the exam." AQA's Paper 2 is a "Written exam: 2 hours 30 minutes" of "Compulsory short-answer and extended-answer questions." AQA's entry options for the A Level are C# (7517A), Java (7517B), Python (7517D) and VB.Net (7517E).

OCR's A Level H446 (OCR now calls itself Cambridge OCR: "As of September 2025, our name is Cambridge OCR.") also has two exams. Computer systems (01) and Algorithms and programming (02) are each a 140-mark, 2 hours and 30 minutes written paper with "no calculators allowed", and each is 40% of the A Level. The Programming project (03 or 04) is non-exam assessment worth 70 marks and 20%. Python is first on OCR's list of programming languages it will accept for the project.

This course teaches the content of both boards in Python, split into the two kinds of thinking the exams test: the programming and algorithms that AQA's Paper 1 and OCR's Paper 02 reward, and the systems theory that AQA's Paper 2 and OCR's Paper 01 reward. Each student works in a batch matched to their board, and every timed paper uses our own original questions written in that board's style. Students practise with the board's free past papers on the board's own website; we never copy board papers or mark schemes into our materials.

The NEA project is the student's own work. AQA asks teachers to sign that "the work is solely that of the student concerned", and OCR's specification says "Students are not allowed help from anyone else. This includes: teachers, parents/carers and other students". So we teach the method on our own practice projects (analysis, design, iterative development, testing and evaluation), and we never write, edit, review or comment on any part of a student's actual NEA. We are independent of AQA and OCR, and we make no promise of grades or university offers.

faqs.question: Which exam boards does this course cover?
faqs.answer: AQA A Level Computer Science (7517) and OCR A Level Computer Science (H446), now branded Cambridge OCR. Students are taught in batches matched to their board, so each timed paper follows the shape of their own exams. A student on another board can ask in the free demo class, but the course is built around these two.

faqs.question: How are the AQA 7517 exams structured?
faqs.answer: AQA lists Paper 1 as an "On-screen exam: 2 hours 30 minutes" worth 40% of the A Level, where students write, adapt and extend programs using AQA's Preliminary Material and Skeleton Program. Paper 2 is a "Written exam: 2 hours 30 minutes" worth 40%. The non-exam assessment project is 75 marks and 20% of the A Level.

faqs.question: How are the OCR H446 exams structured?
faqs.answer: OCR's specification lists Computer systems (01) and Algorithms and programming (02) as 140-mark written papers of 2 hours and 30 minutes each, with no calculators allowed, each worth 40%. The Programming project is non-exam assessment worth 70 marks and 20% of the A Level.

faqs.question: Which programming language do you teach?
faqs.answer: Python. AQA's A Level entry options are C#, Java, Python and VB.Net, and Python is first on OCR's list of languages it accepts for the project. If a school has entered a student for a different AQA language, tell us in the demo class so we can discuss whether this course fits.

faqs.question: Will you help with my NEA project?
faqs.answer: We teach the project method on our own practice projects: choosing a problem, analysis, design, iterative development, testing and evaluation. We never write, edit, review or comment on any part of a student's actual NEA. AQA asks teachers to confirm the work is "solely that of the student concerned", and OCR says "Students are not allowed help from anyone else", so the project must stay entirely the student's own.

faqs.question: Do you use past papers?
faqs.answer: Yes, the way the boards publish them. Students work the boards' free past papers and specimen papers on the boards' own websites and we review their reasoning in class. Our own mocks and practice questions are written by us in each board's style; we never copy board papers or mark schemes into our materials.

faqs.question: Can a Year 13 student join partway through?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Year 13 student joins the current month and also gets a catch-up plan for any earlier topic their school has not covered well. In the final months the course focuses on mocks, weak topics and exam technique for both papers.

faqs.question: Do I need GCSE Computer Science?
faqs.answer: No, but it helps. A student without it should be comfortable with GCSE Maths and willing to program every week. The first month rebuilds Python from solid ground so that nobody is left behind.

faqs.question: Will this course guarantee an A or A* or a university offer?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody honest can promise that. Results depend on the student, the papers and the work they put in. What the course gives is steady programming practice, monthly timed papers with written feedback and a clear plan for each weak topic.

faqs.question: Are you connected with AQA or OCR?
faqs.answer: No. We are an independent online school and are not connected with, endorsed by or approved by AQA, OCR or any exam board. The course follows the boards' published specifications, and students should always check current details with their school and the board.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group batch of 15 to 20 students or 1-on-1. Batches are matched to the student's board. Weekdays or weekends, flexible: choose your batch, or for a very personalised plan choose 1-on-1 at your convenience, weekend mornings or weekdays.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. The first class is free. The teacher works through a short Python task and one theory question with the student, checks their board and year, and recommends a group batch or 1-on-1. There is no obligation to enrol.
